subject: Medicine
summary: Heart block is a spectrum of conduction abnormalities where impulses from atria to ventricles are delayed or blocked. It ranges from first‑degree (prolonged PR) to complete (no conduction). Clinical thinking focuses on identifying the level, severity, and reversible causes to guide urgent treatment.

sections.p: Heart block refers to impaired conduction through the atrioventricular node or His‑Purkinje system. Diagnosis is based on ECG findings: prolonged PR interval (>0.20 s) for first‑degree, dropped QRS for second‑degree, and absence of QRS for third‑degree.
b: First‑degree: PR >0.20 s, all QRS present
Second‑degree type I (Mobitz I): progressive PR prolongation, then dropped QRS
Second‑degree type II (Mobitz II): fixed PR, sudden dropped QRS
Third‑degree: complete dissociation of P waves and QRS

t.b: Shows PR interval, QRS morphology, and relationship of P to QRS; confirms block type and severity

sections.p: Staging follows the degree of block and presence of symptoms. First‑degree is usually asymptomatic; second‑degree may cause syncope; third‑degree often leads to dizziness, heart failure, or sudden death.
b: First‑degree: asymptomatic or mild fatigue
Second‑degree type I: palpitations, syncope
Second‑degree type II: higher risk of progression to complete block
Third‑degree: severe symptoms, risk of sudden death

sections.p: Causes vary from reversible metabolic disturbances to structural heart disease. In low‑resource settings, infections and rheumatic disease are common.
b: Metabolic: hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia
Drug‑induced: beta‑blockers, calcium channel blockers (verapamil), digoxin, amiodarone
Structural: ischemic heart disease, myocarditis, rheumatic heart disease
Infections: HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis

sections.p: Symptoms depend on severity. First‑degree is often silent. Second‑degree can cause dizziness or syncope. Third‑degree leads to fatigue, chest pain, heart failure, or sudden collapse.
b: Palpitations, dizziness, syncope
Chest discomfort, dyspnoea, fatigue
Rapid onset of heart failure signs

sections.p: Beyond ECG, investigations aim to uncover reversible causes and assess haemodynamic impact.
b: Serum electrolytes – rule out hypokalaemia/hyperkalaemia
CBC – look for anemia, infection
Echocardiography – assess structural heart disease
Holter monitoring – detect intermittent block
Blood cultures – if infective endocarditis suspected

t.b: Low → risk of ventricular arrhythmias; high → risk of bradyarrhythmias and block
Yes → consider pacemaker or surgery; no → focus on reversible causes

sections.p: Urgent red flags include syncope, chest pain, or signs of heart failure. Complications can be sudden death or progression to higher‑grade block.
b: Syncope or near‑syncope
Chest pain or dyspnoea
Signs of heart failure (edema, orthopnea)

sections.p: Treat reversible causes first, then provide supportive care. Pacemaker insertion is definitive for symptomatic or high‑grade block.
b: Correct electrolytes – replace potassium or magnesium
Discontinue offending drugs – stop beta‑blockers or verapamil
Treat infections – antibiotics for TB, malaria, etc.
If symptomatic or high‑grade: temporary pacing, then permanent pacemaker

sections.p: Regular ECG monitoring, medication review, and management of underlying conditions reduce recurrence.
b: Annual ECG for known block
Review drugs that affect conduction
Control rheumatic fever, HIV, TB
Patient education on symptom recognition

sections.p: Conditions that mimic bradycardia or conduction delay include sinus bradycardia, atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response, and drug‑induced sinus node dysfunction.
b: Sinus bradycardia – regular rhythm, normal PR
Atrial fibrillation – irregular rhythm, no P waves
Sinus node dysfunction – pauses but normal PR interval

sections.p: Low‑grade block may appear normal on a single ECG; electrolytes can be falsely normal if sampled late.
b: PR interval may be normal in intermittent block
Electrolytes may normalize after correction but still cause block

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden syncope or loss of consciousness
Chest pain or new heart failure symptoms
Rapid deterioration in rhythm or blood pressure

faq.a: Yes, some forms like complete heart block can be familial, but most are acquired.

faq.q: What is the most dangerous type?
faq.a: Complete (third‑degree) block is most dangerous because it can cause sudden death if untreated.

faq.q: Do all patients need a pacemaker?
faq.a: Only symptomatic or high‑grade block patients benefit; low‑grade block often requires no intervention.

exam: Explain the ECG differences between first‑degree, second‑degree type I, second‑degree type II, and third‑degree heart block.
Describe the first‑line management of a patient with symptomatic complete heart block in a low‑resource setting.
List three reversible causes of heart block and how you would investigate each.
